FAQ

## Questions, answered

**Is AI Game Dev really free?**

Yes, the core is free and never expires: the desktop app, the gamedev CLI, the open-source engine plugins for your own AI agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot and others), and image, video and music generation on your own GPU. Hosted chat models inside the app need a paid plan, and Indie starts with a 7-day free trial.

**Which AI models can I use?**

On paid plans you choose the model for each chat. Indie includes Claude Haiku, GPT Luna and DeepSeek. Studio and above add Claude Sonnet, Opus and Fable, GPT Sol, Terra and Astra, and Gemini. With your own agent on the Free plan, you use whatever model that agent runs. Some models are not offered in every country, and a few need age confirmation: the model availability page lists them.

**Which engines and versions are supported?**

Unity 2022.3 LTS or newer, Unreal Engine 5.5 or newer (C++ projects) and Godot 4.3 or newer (.NET): the app installs and connects the right engine plugin for you. The desktop app and the gamedev CLI also create and run BRUTAL (C#, .NET 10), Bevy (Rust; install Rust with rustup) and Three.js web games, and connect the agent to the running game.

**Do I need to write C#, C++ or GDScript myself?**

No. The agent writes and edits the code for you. Your Unity project stays C#; your Godot game code can stay GDScript (the addon needs the .NET build of Godot and the .NET 8 SDK to compile itself); and a Blueprint-only Unreal project needs one C++ class added once, after which you can keep building in Blueprints and the agent can author Blueprints for you.

**Do I need an account or a credit card?**

You sign in with a free AI Game Developer account. The Free plan needs no credit card. Starting the free trial of a paid plan asks for a card, and you can cancel before it ends.

**Is my code used to train AI models?**

We do not collect or store your source code, project files or game assets through the MCP relay; only files you choose to send for image, video, audio or 3D generation are processed. With your own agent, your prompts go straight to your provider. On paid plans our server sends Claude and GPT requests straight to Anthropic and OpenAI, whose API terms say that content is not used for training by default. A few image, video and 3D providers' terms do allow training on the files you send them; the Privacy Policy names every provider and its terms.

**Can I use Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Copilot instead?**

Yes. The Unity, Unreal and Godot plugins are open source under Apache-2.0 and work with any MCP client. A couple of CLI commands install the plugin and configure your agent, and the plugin itself is free.

**Which operating systems are supported?**

The desktop app runs on Windows x64, macOS (Apple silicon and Intel) and Linux x86\_64. The CLI also runs on Linux arm64.

[More answers in the app FAQ →](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/faq)

2. Open it and drag the app into Applications.
3. Start the app from Applications or Launchpad.

### Linux

Use the `.deb` on Debian and Ubuntu based systems, or the AppImage anywhere else:

```bash
# Debian / Ubuntu: use the name of the file you downloaded
sudo apt install ./<downloaded-file>.deb

# Any distribution: make the AppImage executable, then run it
chmod +x ./<downloaded-file>.AppImage
./<downloaded-file>.AppImage
```

**Note**

You do not need Node.js, npm or the engine CLIs for the desktop app. The installers for the Unity, Unreal and Godot plugins ship inside it.

## Install the gamedev CLI

The `gamedev` CLI is the same agent in your terminal. It is published on npm as `@baizor/gamedev` and installs a self-contained prebuilt binary for your platform: Windows x64, macOS arm64 and x64, Linux x64 and arm64.

Requirements: Node.js 22 or newer with npm.

```bash
npm install -g @baizor/gamedev
gamedev --version
```

Then go to your game project and start it:

```bash
cd /path/to/your/game
gamedev
```

You can also run it once without a global install:

```bash
npx @baizor/gamedev
```

On first launch the CLI asks you to sign in. The full command list is in the [CLI reference](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/cli).

## Updates

### Desktop app updates

The desktop app checks for updates on its own. When a new version is available it downloads it in the background and shows **Restart to update**; the update is installed when you restart. You can also check by hand in **Settings**, **About**, which shows the app version and update state.

What changed in each version is on the [release notes page](https://ai-game.dev/releases).

### CLI updates

Update the CLI with one command:

```bash
gamedev update
```

This runs `npm install -g @baizor/gamedev@latest` for you. Inside the interactive CLI, `/update` explains how to upgrade and shows the state of the background service; `/update now` replaces a background service that is waiting to update.

### Package updates

Packages, such as Blender or the Knowledge Base, update separately from the app: they are checked at start-up and every four hours, and you can turn automatic updates off per package. See [Packages](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/packages#updates).

## The background service

The desktop app, the CLI and `gamedev acp` all connect to one AI Game Dev background service on your computer. It owns your sign-in, chats, packages and project files, so a chat keeps running if you close the terminal that started it. You normally never touch it. For a computer that should stay reachable from your other devices, the CLI can install it as a per-user OS service that starts at login:

```bash
gamedev daemon status
gamedev daemon install
```

See the [CLI reference](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/cli#daemon) for the other `daemon` subcommands.

## What gets installed where

- The app keeps its configuration, sign-in and package cache in the `.ai-game-dev` folder in your home directory (`~/.ai-game-dev/`).
- A project gets a `.ai-game-dev/` folder only when something is stored at the project level, for example a package added for the whole team or Knowledge Base notes.
- Local AI models are stored in a model storage folder that you can move to another drive in **Settings**, **Model storage** (or with `/images storage` in the CLI).

# Projects and engines

Open or create a Unity, Unreal or Godot project in the AI Game Dev app, install the engine plugin, and let the agent open the editor when needed.

_Last updated: 2026-11-14_

Everything in the AI Game Dev app happens inside a project: a folder on your computer. When the folder is a Unity, Unreal Engine or Godot project, the app detects the engine, sets up the matching MCP plugin and connects the editor's tools to your chat. This page covers opening and creating projects in the desktop app and the CLI, plugin installation and updates, and how the agent works with the editor.

## Supported engines

| Engine | Plugin | How the app recognises the project | Supported versions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unity | [Unity MCP](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/unity) | `ProjectSettings/ProjectVersion.txt`, or an `Assets/` folder with `Packages/manifest.json` | Unity 2022.3 LTS or newer |
| Unreal Engine | [Unreal MCP](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/unreal) | A `*.uproject` file in the folder | Unreal Engine 5.5 or newer, C++ projects |
| Godot | [Godot MCP](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/godot) | A `project.godot` file in the folder | Godot 4.3 or newer (.NET) |

You can also open any other folder, such as a Blender-only asset project, a design docs folder or a tools repository. The agent can then work with files, packages and tools, just without engine tools.

## Open a project in the desktop app

An empty window is a launcher. It offers:

- **Open folder…** to choose a project folder.
- **Create new project** to start a new Unity, Unreal or Godot project.
- Your recent projects.

Each project lives in its own window. Ctrl-click (Windows, Linux) or Cmd-click (macOS) a recent project to open it in a new window instead of replacing the current one. When you relaunch the app, every project window that was open comes back with its size, position and layout.

## Install or update the engine plugin

After you open an engine project, the sidebar shows the project's engine and its actions:

- **Install Package** when the engine plugin is not in the project yet, or **Update Package** when a newer plugin version is available.
- **Open Editor** to start the engine editor for this project.

Click **Install Package** to add the plugin. The app never changes an existing project on its own: the click is your consent, because the install writes into your project (for Unity, for example, it adds the package to `Packages/manifest.json`). When a project is created from the app, the plugin is installed automatically as part of creation.

The plugin installers ship inside the app: you do not need Node.js, npm, `unity-mcp-cli`, `unreal-mcp-cli` or `godot-cli` on your machine.

In the CLI the same actions are slash commands:

```text
/install-plugin            install the MCP plugin into the current project
/install-plugin C:/Games/MyGame
/open                      open the editor for the current project
```

## Engine extensions

Engine extensions add more tools to a plugin, for example extra Unity tools for particle systems or animation. Browse and install them from the sidebar's extensions action in the desktop app, or with `/install-extension` in the CLI. The [extensions page](https://ai-game.dev/docs/extensions) lists what is available for each engine.

## Create a new project

In the desktop app, choose **Create new project**:

1. Pick the engine.
2. Enter a project name. The project is created in a subfolder with that name inside the parent folder you choose; missing folders are created.
3. Pick the editor: the newest installed version is preselected, or choose an installed editor by hand. If no editor for that engine is installed, the app says so; install the engine first, then continue.
4. The app creates the project, installs the plugin and opens it.

In the CLI:

```text
/create-project unity SkywardKeep
/create-project godot SkywardKeep D:/Games
```

The syntax is `/create-project <unity|godot|unreal> <name> [parentDir]`.

## How the agent works with the editor

You can start chatting before the editor is running. Ordinary discussion never launches anything. When the agent needs the editor for a task, it asks the app to open the project's editor, waits until the editor's tools are available and then continues the same task. An editor that comes online later in a session, for example because you opened it yourself, is connected to the running chat without starting a new one.

A few rules keep this predictable:

- Only one editor is started per project, even if several sessions need it at the same time.
- An engine call that was already sent is never replayed automatically after a disconnect; the agent checks the result before trying another write.
- **Stop** cancels a wait for the editor. An editor that has already started stays open.
- Starting a large project can take a while. A launch is given up to 15 minutes, then up to 2 more minutes for the tools to appear.

**Tip**

Opening the editor before you start a long session saves the start-up wait on the first engine step.

## Inside the editor

Each plugin has its own window in the editor (for Unity, the **AI Game Developer** window) with the connection status. When the app opens the editor, it passes your signed-in session, so the plugin connects through ai-game.dev without a manual token. If the editor shows "Disconnected", open that window, choose **Cloud** and click **Authorize**, then wait for **Ready**.

Plugin-specific settings, manual installation and connecting other AI clients are covered in each engine's wiki:

- Unity: [installation](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/unity/installation), [connecting AI clients](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/unity/connecting-ai-clients), [`unity-mcp-cli`](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/unity/cli).
- Unreal: [installation](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/unreal/installation), [connecting AI clients](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/unreal/connecting-ai-clients), [`unreal-mcp-cli`](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/unreal/cli).
- Godot: [installation](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/godot/installation), [connecting AI clients](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/godot/connecting-ai-clients), [`godot-cli`](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/godot/cli).

## Open a project in the CLI

The CLI works in the current directory, or in a folder you name:

```bash
cd /path/to/your/game
gamedev

# or
gamedev /path/to/your/game
gamedev --project /path/to/your/game
```

On start, the CLI says what it detected, for example "Unity project detected", or that the folder has no Unity, Godot or Unreal project.

## What the agent can do in your project

With an engine connected, ask in plain language, for example:

- "List everything in the active scene."
- "Create a cube at the origin and give it a physics body."
- "Take a screenshot of the current view."

The [tools catalog](https://ai-game.dev/docs/tools) lists every engine tool, and the [best practices](https://ai-game.dev/docs/best-practices) explain how to write requests that work. The engine pages for [Unity](https://ai-game.dev/engines/unity), [Unreal](https://ai-game.dev/engines/unreal) and [Godot](https://ai-game.dev/engines/godot) summarise each integration.

# gamedev CLI reference

Every gamedev CLI command and option: interactive and headless modes, pkg, remote, daemon, acp, image-runtime, update, and the slash commands in the terminal.

_Last updated: 2026-11-04_

The `gamedev` CLI is the AI Game Dev agent in your terminal: the same account, models, packages and engine connection as the desktop app. This reference lists every command and option of the CLI, the slash commands you type inside it, and its exit codes. Install it with `npm install -g @baizor/gamedev` (see [Installation](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/installation#cli)).

## Usage at a glance

```text
gamedev [<project-dir>] [options]          interactive terminal UI
gamedev --print "<prompt>"                 headless one-shot query, reply on stdout
gamedev --print -                          headless, prompt read from stdin
gamedev --headless                         headless, prompt read from stdin
gamedev update                             upgrade the CLI to the latest version
gamedev pkg <subcommand> [args]            manage packages, then exit
gamedev image-runtime [status|start]       the local image runtime
gamedev remote <subcommand> [args]         remote access and your other devices
gamedev daemon <subcommand>                the background service
gamedev --on <name|id-prefix>              the terminal UI on another computer's chats
gamedev acp [--model <model>]              Agent Client Protocol agent on stdin/stdout
gamedev --help | --version
```

## Options

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `<project-dir>` | Project folder (same as `--project`); a relative path is resolved against the current directory |
| `--project`, `-p <path>` | Project folder (default: the current directory) |
| `--cwd <path>` | Alias for `--project` |
| `--model <model>` | Model to use (default: the one your account is assigned) |
| `--resume`, `-r <id>` | Resume a previous session |
| `--print <prompt>` | Non-interactive: send the prompt, stream the reply to stdout, exit. `-` reads stdin |
| `--headless` | Force non-interactive mode, prompt from stdin |
| `--on <name>` | Open the terminal UI on another paired computer's chats |
| `--help`, `-h` | Show help |
| `--version`, `-v` | Print the version |

`--project` and `--cwd` take precedence over a positional folder.

## Interactive mode

Run `gamedev` in a project folder. Type a request and press Enter. Useful keys:

- `/` opens the slash command palette; arrow keys move, Tab completes the command name.
- Esc while a reply is streaming interrupts it.
- Ctrl+C exits (press twice to confirm).
- Hold Space for about a third of a second in the input to talk (push-to-talk voice input).

Without a terminal (piped input) the CLI falls back to a simple line mode.

## Headless mode and scripting

Headless runs print only the reply on stdout; what the CLI detected (for example "Unity project detected") goes to stderr.

```bash
gamedev --print "List every scene in this project"
echo "Summarise the open TODOs in Assets/Scripts" | gamedev --headless
gamedev --project ./MyGame --model <model-id> --print "Run the edit-mode tests"
```

| Exit code | When |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | The reply finished |
| `1` | A query, network or agent error, or Ctrl+C after the run started |
| `2` | Not signed in, an empty prompt, or an unusable folder or flag |
| `130` | Ctrl+C before the run started; nothing was sent |
| `143` | SIGTERM; the CLI detaches and a prompt already sent keeps running in the background service |

## gamedev pkg

Manage [packages](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/packages) of the project in the current directory (or `--cwd <path>`). Level flags: `--user` (every project on this computer), `--project` (committed, the default), `--local` (this checkout only).

```text
gamedev pkg list [--user]                      packages in effect (--user: the user level alone)
gamedev pkg add <input> [level]                <publisher.name>[@range] | github:<owner>/<repo>[@tag|#ref] | npm:<name> | file:<path> | URL | owner/repo | folder
gamedev pkg remove <id> [level]                delete the id's entry at that level
gamedev pkg exclude <id> [level]               turn the package off at that level
gamedev pkg include <id> [level]               undo exclude
gamedev pkg update [<id>] [--user]             newest compatible version within the declared range, now
gamedev pkg auto-update on|off <id>            this computer's auto-update preference for one package
gamedev pkg sync [--user]                      make locks and cache match the level files
gamedev pkg link <folder> [level]              use a local folder instead of the published version (default --local)
gamedev pkg unlink <id> [level]                stop using the local folder
gamedev pkg dev <folder> [level]               link, and rebuild on every source change until Ctrl+C
gamedev pkg settings <id> [<key> [<value>]]    read or write a package's settings (--unset clears a value)
```

`gamedev pkg settings` exits with code 1 when a value is refused and 2 on a usage error. See [Creating packages](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/creating-packages#develop) for `link` and `dev`.

## gamedev image-runtime

```text
gamedev image-runtime status [--json]    show this computer's local image runtime coordinator
gamedev image-runtime start [--json]     start it through the background service
```

Models themselves are managed with `/images` inside the CLI (below).

## gamedev remote

Remote access between your computers and devices signed in to the same account. `/remote` in the interactive CLI is the same command.

```text
gamedev remote status                         this computer and your other devices
gamedev remote pair                           show a pairing code and QR, then approve the device that enters it
gamedev remote join <device> <code>           pair with another computer
gamedev remote allow [<device>]               allow remote control here, or let a device control chats
gamedev remote allow <device> --services      let a device use this computer's shared models
gamedev remote block [<device>] [--services]  turn remote control off, or take a device's access away
gamedev remote share [on|off]                 share this computer's models with your other computers
gamedev remote share pause|resume             stop or resume accepting images from other computers
gamedev remote forget <device>                unpin a computer you paired with
gamedev remote revoke <device>                remove a device paired with this computer
gamedev remote rename <name>                  the name your other devices see
```

A device is a name or the start of its id. `pair` asks separately about viewing, control and shared models. Then `gamedev --on <device>` opens that computer's chats; `/machine` lists or switches computers and `/machine this` comes back.

## gamedev daemon

The background service that the desktop app and the CLI share.

```text
gamedev daemon status       installed and running; the Kernel, account, remote access, logs
gamedev daemon install      run it as a per-user OS service that starts at login and restarts if it stops
gamedev daemon uninstall    remove the OS service
gamedev daemon start        start the background service
gamedev daemon stop         stop it
gamedev daemon restart      stop, then start
gamedev daemon logs [kernel|service|remote|auth] [--lines N] [--follow]
```

The OS service is a LaunchAgent on macOS, a systemd user unit on Linux and a Task Scheduler task at logon on Windows; it needs no admin rights.

## gamedev acp

`gamedev acp` turns the CLI into an Agent Client Protocol agent for ACP clients such as T3 Code, Zed and JetBrains IDEs. The client starts it; protocol messages use stdout and diagnostics go to stderr. In the client, add a custom agent with the command `gamedev` and the argument `acp`. It uses this computer's sign-in, your account's models and the project's engine tools. The post [AI Game Dev as an ACP agent in T3 Code](https://ai-game.dev/blog/acp-agent-t3-code) walks through the setup.

## Slash commands

Type these inside the interactive CLI. Many also work in the desktop chat.

### Chat and session

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/help` | List the available commands |
| `/clear` | Start a fresh conversation |
| `/reset` | Reset the current session |
| `/reopen` | Reopen a lost chat from its saved history (nothing is resent) |
| `/saved` | Recover saved messages, settings, images and file or Git changes |
| `/model` | Pick the model (Tab: reasoning effort) |
| `/agent` | List the agents; `/agent use <id>` switches, `/agent refresh` reloads the list |
| `/skills` | List the skills available in this project |
| `/context` | Toggle the context debug panel |
| `/exit` | Exit (also `/quit`) |

### Account, settings and updates

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/login [--switch]` | Sign in; `--switch` changes this computer's account |
| `/logout` | Sign out |
| `/config` | Settings, including this session's **Tools** |
| `/permissions` | Show or change when the AI asks before running tools |
| `/voice-language` | Set the voice transcription language |
| `/update [now]` | How to upgrade the CLI; `now` updates a waiting background service |
| `/remote`, `/machine` | Remote access; list or switch computers |

### Engine and project

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/install-plugin [path]` | Install the MCP plugin into the current Unity, Godot or Unreal project |
| `/install-extension` | Browse and install an engine extension |
| `/open` | Open the editor for the current project |
| `/create-project` | Create a new game project, for example `/create-project unity MyGame` (engine `unity`, `godot` or `unreal`, a name, an optional parent folder) |
| `/file` | Create, rename, move, copy or delete project files |
| `/files [n]` | List files mentioned in this chat; open one |
| `/search`, `/replace` | Search the project; save, apply and recover Search Replace |
| `/git` | Status, stage, commit, discard, pull, push, force-push and init |

### Extensions, packages and models

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/packages` | The same subcommands as `gamedev pkg`, plus `views`, `tree <view id>`, `runs`, `cancel` and `reload` |
| `/mcp` | Manage the project's MCP servers: add, enable, remove, test |
| `/plugin` | Manage Claude plugins and marketplaces: install, enable, update |
| `/images` | Local image models, downloads and storage (`/images help`) |
| `/image [n]` | List this session's images; open or remove one |
| `/models` | Every way to run a media model, local and cloud; add `image`, `video`, `audio` or `3d` (`/models help`) |
| `/cloud` | This session's Cloud generation setting: `ask`, `budget <percent>` or `off` |
| `/blender`, `/supercollider`, `/kb` | Commands of the Blender, Music and Knowledge Base packages |

Installed packages can add more slash commands; they appear in the `/` palette.

### /images subcommands

```text
/images                               this computer, the runtime, storage and every image model
/images download <model> [--yes]      download a model (and the runtime when missing); asks first
/images cancel|resume <model|runtime> stop or continue a download
/images update <model> [--yes]        download a model's update
/images delete <model> [--yes]        delete a model's files from this computer
/images allow|block <model> [--user|--project]   whether the agent may use it
/images default <model|auto>          the default image model (auto = recommended for this computer)
/images stop [session|<job id>]       stop image generation and free the GPU
/images free-space [--yes]            delete model files no model uses any more
/images storage [<new folder>]        show or move the model storage folder
/images redetect                      detect the GPU, memory and driver again
/images reinstall                     set the image runtime up again
```

## Environment variables

| Variable | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `AI_GAME_DEV_MODEL` | Default model override |
| `AI_GAME_DEV_ASCII_GLYPHS` | `1` forces ASCII meters in the `/model` picker for terminals that mis-measure emoji |

Configuration priority: command-line options, then environment variables, then `~/.ai-game-dev/config.json`.

## Related

- The engine plugins have their own CLIs: [`unity-mcp-cli`](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/unity/cli), [`unreal-mcp-cli`](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/unreal/cli), [`godot-cli`](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/godot/cli).
- [Troubleshooting](https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/troubleshooting) for errors and exit codes in practice.

Reports go to our **self-hosted** error-tracking service (GlitchTip, a Sentry-compatible tool) on our own infrastructure and are not shared with third parties. We keep them for **90 days**, after which they are deleted automatically. We process them on the basis of our legitimate interest in finding and fixing defects and running a reliable, secure service (Section 3). Turning reports off is the simplest way to object to this processing; you can also object, or ask us to delete reports already sent, at [[REDACTED-EMAIL]](mailto:[REDACTED-EMAIL]).

### 2.11 AI Request Records

For each AI request we proxy (Section 2.8) we keep records **about** the request. They do not contain your prompts or the AI's output:

- **Provider attempt records** — the provider we sent the request to (and, if a request is retried with another provider, each attempt), the model requested and the model sent to the provider, when the request was sent, how long it took (to the first output and in total), the token counts (input, output, and prompt-cache reads and writes), the HTTP status, the type of any error, and the provider's request identifier. They are linked to your account.
- **Usage records** — for each request that consumed tokens, the model you asked for, the model and provider that served it, the token counts (input, output, and prompt-cache reads and writes), what the request cost and what was charged for it, a request identifier, the type, version and platform of the app or tool that sent it, and, if your first request after switching AI model followed a usage-limit card or a model suggestion in the app, which of the two prompted the switch (the "switch source"). They are linked to your account.

We use these records to bill your usage, to measure each provider's availability, speed and error rate so that requests can be routed as described in Section 2.8, and to diagnose errors. We also use the switch source in aggregate internal reports to measure whether those prompts help people keep using the Service. It is sent whether or not "Share usage data" (Section 2.15) is on, and is not shared with third parties. How long we keep these records is set out in Section 7.

### 2.12 Website Analytics and How You Found Us

Our website counts visits and a few actions on its pages with self-hosted analytics (Section 10): which pages were viewed, which download or sign-in button was used, when an installation command or code example is copied, and the steps of signing up and checking out. These counts use **no cookies**. The only browser storage involved is a marker kept for the current tab when you return from a card checkout, so that one purchase is not counted twice.

When you create an account we also record **how you first reached us**: the campaign parameters in the link you arrived on (`utm_source`, `utm_medium`, `utm_campaign`, `utm_term`, `utm_content`), the domain (not the full address) of the website that referred you, and the path of the first page you opened. Your browser keeps this only in memory until you sign up; nothing is stored on your device. It is stored with your account.

Our servers additionally record account events for analytics: that an account was created and how (email or a named sign-in provider), that an email address was verified, which kind of client signed in (our desktop app or CLI, an engine plugin, or another MCP client by its registered name) and whether it was the account's first, and that a purchase was confirmed with its plan, net amount and currency. These events identify the account only by a one-way pseudonymous code, never by name or email, and carry the traffic source above. The same code is used for the product-usage events that the desktop app and command-line tool send to Umami (Section 2.15); the product-usage events in our own database use a different, random identifier. When you delete your account, we replace that code with a fixed value on these events and on the product-usage events held in Umami, so we can no longer find them by your account, and we do not try to link them back. They are not anonymous: a purchase event still carries its time, plan and amount, which could be matched to our billing records (Section 7). We also count desktop app downloads served from our site by platform and version, without any account link.

### 2.13 Image, Video, Audio and 3D Generation (Paid Plans)

On paid plans you can ask the Service to generate or transform images, video, audio (speech, sound effects and music) and 3D models. This is not available on the free tier or during the free trial. **What is sent.** To run a request we send the provider that serves it the text of your prompt (and negative prompt, if any) or the text to be spoken, the generation settings (such as duration, resolution, aspect ratio, voice and seed) and any images or other files you chose to provide — for example first and last frames, reference images, an image to edit, or a 3D model to texture or convert. We do **not** send your email address, your IP address or the identifiers described in Section 2.9, and except for image requests to OpenAI (below) we do not send your account identifier; the provider sees a request from our servers carrying our own credentials, not one from your device.

**Our copy.** Files you upload for generation, and the results, are stored privately on our servers and linked to your account, and are deleted automatically after **7 days** — except files you upload to Tripo and everything Tripo returns (3D models and images, below), which are **not yet deleted automatically**: we keep them until you ask us to delete them at [[REDACTED-EMAIL]](mailto:[REDACTED-EMAIL]). A record that a file existed (its name, type, size, checksum and dates, but not its content) remains with your usage records. The text of your request is kept with the record of that request for no longer than the billing records of the usage (Section 7); the text of a price quote you did not go ahead with is not yet deleted automatically. Results are not shared with anyone else.

**Providers.** We may choose the provider for each request, and if the chosen provider rejects it we may send it to another provider listed here for the **same model**:

- **fal** (**fal – Features & Labels, Inc.**; United States) — the main route for most video models and for audio generation. fal processes data in the United States and other countries. Its documentation states that it keeps request inputs and outputs in its request history for up to **90 days** by default, and that media files stay on its servers for a period set per request or per account, for which it publishes no fixed default. Its terms allow it to use anonymized or aggregated data derived from customer input to develop its products and AI models; they do not say whether it trains models on the content itself. We have **not agreed no-training or zero-retention terms** with fal.
- **Runway** (**Runway AI, Inc.**; United States) — serves some video models and is the failover route for others. **Runway's terms state that inputs and outputs may be used by Runway to train and improve its AI models**, and we have not agreed different terms with Runway. Runway's result links are temporary, and it publishes no retention period for inputs that we could find. Requests from accounts in the EU/EEA, the United Kingdom or Switzerland are **never sent to Runway**, and neither are requests from accounts whose country we cannot determine.
- **Google** (**Google LLC**; United States) — the failover route for Veo video models, through Vertex AI, and only for accounts whose holder has confirmed they are at least 18. Unlike Gemini, Veo requests are sent to Google's **us-central1** location in the United States rather than its global endpoint. The description of Google's no-training terms and abuse-monitoring logs in Section 2.8 applies. Google publishes no separate retention period for Veo that we could find.
- **OpenAI** (Section 2.8) — serves image generation and editing with OpenAI's image models. With these requests we also send **our internal identifier for your account** (a random code, not your name or email address), which OpenAI uses to detect misuse of its service. OpenAI's terms and retention described in Section 2.8 apply.
- **Tripo** (tripo3d.ai) — serves 3D generation and the image generation and editing steps it offers for 3D work. Tripo's website terms name Holymolly Limited as the operator of its service, and its technology is developed by VAST, a company based in China. Tripo's published materials do not let us confirm which entity contracts with API customers, where API data is processed (including whether that is China), or how long it is kept. Its terms treat free and paid users differently on the use of content to improve its models, and we have not agreed separate terms with Tripo. Requests from accounts in the EU/EEA, the United Kingdom or Switzerland are **never sent to Tripo**, and neither are requests from accounts whose country we cannot determine.

**Model developers.** Many video models are developed by other companies (for example ByteDance, Kuaishou, Alibaba, MiniMax, Tencent, Lightricks and Google). The developer is not necessarily the company that processes your request, but fal and Runway offer some models through partners, and neither tells us, model by model, where partner-operated models run. **For some models your request may therefore be processed by the model's developer, including in China.** Requests from accounts in the EU/EEA, the United Kingdom or Switzerland are sent only to models that are not operated by a company based in China.

**Your files.** Do not upload images of identifiable people unless you are entitled to and they have agreed, and do not upload anything you cannot share with these providers.

### 2.14 Mobile Apps (iOS and Android)

**Sign-in.** To sign in, the app shows a short code and opens the ai-game.dev sign-in page in your browser, where you sign in with your ai-game.dev account and confirm the code. The app never sees your password. It then stores its session credentials in your phone's secure storage (the iOS Keychain, or app-private storage encrypted with a key held by the Android Keystore). When you sign in we record the IP address and user-agent of the session, as described in Section 2.5.

**Pairing and your phone's record.** To connect your phone to your computers, the app creates a key pair on the phone (the private key never leaves it) and registers the phone with your account. We store one record per phone: a random device ID created for your account (not your advertising identifier or a hardware identifier), a device name, the platform, the phone's public key, the capabilities the app reports, and a "last seen" time that the app refreshes while it is open so your computers can show whether the phone is online. On iOS the device name is only the type of device, such as "iPhone" or "iPad"; on Android it is the device name set in your phone's settings (or "Android" and the model if none is set). Your paired computers can show this name. You pair a computer by scanning a QR code or typing a code, and confirming on the computer.

**Your computer's record.** When you turn on remote control in the AI Game Dev desktop app, it registers your computer with your account in the same way: a random device ID, a device name (by default your computer's network na

**Caveat:** The text you provided omits Section 2.13 (media generation) and Section 2.8 (AI request routing). Where I describe 2.13 below, I rely on references to it in other sections.

## Data collected and stored
- **Account and device data:** Phone and computer records (including a computer's public key and a "last seen" time) are kept while your account exists.
- **Chats and images:** Messages, attachments, approvals and replies travel only between your phone and your computer over an end-to-end encrypted connection. The policy says they "do not pass through our servers in readable form."
- **Phone cache:** Recent chats and unsent messages are stored on the phone and deleted on sign-out or uninstall.
- **Camera:** iOS uses the camera only to scan the pairing QR code, and the image is not stored or sent to you.
- **Biometrics:** Face ID, Touch ID and fingerprint checks happen on the phone. Not stated as sent to the provider, and the policy says the provider never receives biometric data.
- **Mobile apps:** The policy says they contain no analytics SDK, crash reporter or tracking.

## Do project source code or assets go to servers?
Not stated directly. The policy says AI requests are proxied to providers on paid plans and the free trial, but what those requests contain is in Section 2.8, which is not included. Analytics explicitly exclude prompts, file paths, and project, asset and file names. Agent problem reports may include a free-text description written by the agent that "could contain information from your session."

## The relay logs
The policy does not describe an "MCP relay." It describes a **TURN relay** (turn.ai-game.dev) that forwards encrypted WebRTC traffic when devices cannot connect directly. The relay:
- Cannot read or store the packets.
- Logs sessions with a relay user name (built from account and device IDs) and device IP addresses.
- Keeps running byte counters per relay user name until restart.
- Retention: logs are overwritten "usually within days" and are **not deleted** when you delete your account. Counters are discarded on restart. Monthly byte counts per device are deleted with your account.

## Providers and what each receives
- **Paddle:** Billing data. Merchant of record for new purchases.
- **Stripe:** Billing data for legacy subscriptions only.
- **Anthropic, OpenAI, Google:** Proxied AI requests on paid plans and the free trial. Free-tier traffic is never sent to them. Request contents: not stated here.
- **DeepInfra:** Paid chat requests to DeepSeek-family models. For EU/EEA/UK/Swiss accounts, receives web-search queries and result extracts for summarising.
- **Sail Research:** Paid requests to DeepSeek-family models and, when available, GLM models, for non-EU/EEA/UK/Swiss accounts.
- **Jasnah (NEAR AI):** Paid requests to GLM models only, when available.
- **Google (Gemini, Veo):** Gemini for Studio-plan-and-above accounts confirmed 18+, excluding EU/EEA/UK/Swiss accounts. Veo for accounts confirmed 18+.
- **fal, Runway, Tripo:** Prompts, settings and files for video, audio and 3D generation. Runway and Tripo receive nothing from EU/EEA/UK/Swiss accounts.
- **DeepSeek:** Web-search queries only, for non-EU/EEA/UK/Swiss accounts. Receives the query, a fixed instruction, a session ID and an installation ID. Processing occurs in **China**.
- **Brave:** Query text only, for EU/EEA/UK/Swiss accounts. No user ID or IP address.
- **Apple (APNs), Google (Firebase, Play services):** Push tokens, identifiers and, for Android, device details. Notifications contain no chat content. Google's code scanner may send diagnostic data.
- **Cloudflare:** Encrypted backups and analytics exports (R2 storage).
- **Hosting provider:** Infrastructure only.
- **Self-hosted (no third party):** Email, Umami analytics, GlitchTip crash reporting, and the product-analytics database.

## Retention periods
- Billing and tax records: at least 7 years (about 10 for EU VAT).
- Consent and purchase evidence: 6 years after the relevant period ends.
- Sign-up records: 6 years after account deletion, or later if you paid.
- Free-trial card hashes: 24 months after last use.
- AI provider attempt records: 60 days.
- Generation uploads and results: 7 days, except Tripo files, which are kept until you ask for deletion.
- Crash and error reports: 90 days.
- Product-usage analytics: 24 months.
- Local analytics queue on your computer: up to 30 days.
- Backups: daily 15 days, weekly 57 days, monthly 366 days.
- Connection signalling data: until the attempt expires.
- Verification tokens: 48 hours (email) and 1 hour (password reset).
- Operational logs: rolling 90-day window, with no fixed deletion guarantee.

## Use for training
- **Your data (general):** Not stated.
- **Agent problem reports:** The policy says they are "not" used "to train AI models."
- **Third-party terms:** Runway's terms reportedly permit using inputs and outputs for training. The policy does not say whether other providers train on data.

## Section 2.13 (media generation)
Section 2.13 itself is not in the text provided. Other sections indicate:
- Prompts, settings and files go to fal (video/audio), Runway (video, non-EU) and Tripo (3D, non-EU).
- Veo requests go to Google's US location.
- Uploaded files and results are deleted after 7 days, except Tripo files.

## AI Game Developer (ai-game.dev): facts from the pages

**Bottom line for a Three.js 0.180 + Spark project:** the pages I read say the product supports Three.js, but none of them describe how it works with an existing Three.js project, which tools the agent gets for Three.js, or whether it runs headless on Linux. Those are "not stated" below. The only Three.js-specific statements are marketing lines.

### (1) What it is, and engine support

- **Desktop app plus CLI, with a hosted MCP endpoint.** The download page offers a desktop app (Windows x64, macOS Apple silicon and Intel, Linux x86_64) and a CLI installed with `npm install -g @baizor/gamedev`. Source: https://ai-game.dev/download and https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/installation
- **Also an MCP server.** It is hosted at `https://ai-game.dev/mcp`, using Streamable HTTP. Source: https://ai-game.dev/mcp-endpoint-info
- **Engine plugins.** Unity, Unreal and Godot plugins are installed by the app or CLI, and they are the engines with an MCP tool count (72, 98 and 47). Source: https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/projects-and-engines
- **Not a cloud IDE.** Nothing I read describes a browser IDE. The homepage calls it "a free desktop app."
- **Three.js wording, exact:**
  - Homepage, "Six engines, one app": "plus BRUTAL, Bevy and Three.js, which the app creates, builds and runs for you."
  - FAQ: the app and CLI "also create and run BRUTAL (C#, .NET 10), Bevy (Rust; install Rust with rustup) and Three.js web games, and connect the agent to the running game."
  - Homepage step 2: "Pick a new or existing Unity, Unreal, Godot, BRUTAL, Bevy or Three.js project."
  - Sources: https://ai-game.dev/ and https://ai-game.dev/ FAQ section
- **Three.js is absent from the engine-specific docs.** The supported-engines table on https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/projects-and-engines lists only Unity, Unreal and Godot. Three.js has no install guide, no MCP setup command and no Three.js tool list in any page I read. Its Three.js page was not linked from the pages I read.

### (2) Existing project, or only new ones?

- **Existing projects are claimed, but not detailed.** The homepage says to pick "a new or existing" Three.js project. Nothing says whether a Vite/TypeScript project, or a standalone HTML page using three.js 0.180 and @sparkjsdev/spark with .glb models, is detected or supported.
- **Any folder can be opened.** The projects page says: "You can also open any other folder... The agent can then work with files, packages and tools, just without engine tools." Whether a Three.js folder counts as an "engine tools" case is not stated.
- **Create and open flows** (for Unity, Unreal and Godot only, per the same page): "Open folder…" in the app, or `gamedev /path/to/your/game` in the CLI.

### (3) How it connects to Claude Code

- **Command, from https://ai-game.dev/mcp-endpoint-info:** `claude mcp add --transport http ai-game-dev "https://ai-game.dev/mcp"`
- **Auth:** OAuth 2.1 browser sign-in. A personal access token can be used instead, via an `Authorization: Bearer` header.
- **Project pinning:** `/mcp/p/<pin>` is pinned to one project. It is written by `setup-mcp`, which exists only for `unity-mcp-cli`, `unreal-mcp-cli` and `godot-cli`. No Three.js equivalent is documented.
- **Tool names for Three.js:** not stated. The only published names are examples, such as "Screenshot / Isolated GameObject" and "Console / Get Logs" (Godot). The full catalogue is at https://ai-game.dev/docs/tools, which I did not fetch.
- **Playtest and input features** (screenshot, input events, video recording, scene graph, transforms, materials): not stated for Three.js. The homepage says the agent "enters Play mode, reads console errors and takes screenshots" (Unity/Unreal/Godot context).

### (4) Linux and headless

- **Linux desktop:** AppImage and .deb, x86_64 only. "No arm64 Linux build yet." Source: https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/installation
- **CLI on Linux:** prebuilt binaries for x64 and arm64. It needs Node.js 22 or newer. Note that the download page says "Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+", which does not match the installation page.
- **Headless mode exists for prompts, not rendering.** `gamedev --print "<prompt>"` and `--headless` send a prompt and print the reply. The CLI reference does not say the game is rendered headless. Source: https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/cli
- **Software WebGL, display requirements, GPU requirements for the game:** not stated.
- **Browser extension:** none mentioned.
- **Account needed:** yes. "On first launch the CLI asks you to sign in." This also applies on the Free plan.
- **Hosted dependency:** the app and CLI require sign-in to the hosted service. The Free plan works with your own agent, but prompts go straight to your provider. Paid AI goes through their servers.

### (5) Pricing, free tier, credits

Source: https://ai-game.dev/pricing (last updated 2026-10-17), with the plan terms in https://ai-game.dev/legal/terms.

- **Free:** $0. "Bring your own AI agent. Pay your AI provider directly." Includes "Unlimited MCP server access" and "Unreal, Unity, Godot & Blender." Three.js is not in the feature list. Account needed, no card.
- **Indie:** $25/month ($24/month or $285/year billed annually). Hosted Claude Haiku and GPT Luna.
- **Studio:** $99/month ($94/month or $1129/year). Claude Opus, Sonnet and Fable, and GPT models.
- **Studio Max:** $199/month ($189/month or $2269/year). More than 8× Indie's usage.
- **Indie trial:** 7 days, requires a card, and auto-renews at $25 after the trial unless cancelled.
- **Usage:** a weekly allowance applies to paid plans. Optional pay-as-you-go extended usage is funded from a prepaid balance, with a 15% markup on provider cost.
- **Billing:** Paddle is merchant of record. Taxes are added at checkout.
- **Caveat:** the Terms say a usage charge is made "whether or not the result was useful," and an agent that keeps running consumes allowance.

### (6) Privacy and terms

Sources: https://ai-game.dev/trust, https://ai-game.dev/legal/privacy (Privacy Policy version 3.10, effective 21 November 2026) and https://ai-game.dev/legal/terms (version 3.8 applies now).

- **Project code and assets through the relay:** the Privacy Policy, section 2.7, says the company does not collect, store or access "Your source code, project files, or game assets." The relay "routes tool calls ... without inspecting or persisting the payload contents."
- **What the relay does log:** tool calls, timing and status (section 2.5), and MCP events including "the tool, prompt, or resource referenced" (section 2.6).
- **Paid AI requests:** the prompt "including any code or other project context your AI agent adds" goes to the provider that serves the model. Providers include Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepInfra and Sail Research (section 2.8).
- **Free plan with your own agent:** prompts do not pass through the company's servers (section 2.8).
- **Training:** Anthropic's commercial terms say it may not train on API content. OpenAI keeps request content up to 30 days for abuse monitoring, and "not used for training by default." Runway's terms reportedly permit training on inputs and outputs. The Privacy Policy says general use for training is "Not stated" (from the model summary).
- **Media generation uploads:** deleted after 7 days, except Tripo files, which are kept until you ask for deletion (section 2.13).
- **Crash reports:** sent by default, can be turned off. They may name a file or folder, or quote short text (sections 2.7 and 2.10).
- **Retention, from the Privacy Policy summary:** crash reports 90 days, AI provider attempt records 60 days, product analytics 24 months, backups up to 366 days. This comes from a model-extracted summary, not verbatim text.
- **Ownership:** Terms section 10 says you keep your rights in "your projects, source code, game assets, and any content you create," and "we claim none of them."
- **Agent actions, Terms section 2.2:** the software and AI agents "can ... read, create, modify, overwrite and delete files, folders and entire projects," and "Some of these actions cannot be undone."
- **Governing law:** Washington State, USA.
- **Contacts:** [REDACTED-EMAIL], [REDACTED-EMAIL], [REDACTED-EMAIL].
- **Not fetched:** the Refund & Cancellation Policy at https://ai-game.dev/legal/refund.

### (7) Licence, maker, and age

- **Open source:** the Unity, Godot and Unreal plugins, the GameDev-MCP-Server and MCP-Plugin-dotnet are Apache-2.0 (Terms section 9). Repos: https://github.com/IvanMurzak/Unity-MCP, https://github.com/IvanMurzak/Godot-MCP, https://github.com/IvanMurzak/Unreal-MCP, https://github.com/IvanMurzak/GameDev-MCP-Server, https://github.com/IvanMurzak/MCP-Plugin-dotnet.
- **Proprietary:** the desktop app, the hosted service and the rest of the Software. Three.js support is not listed as open source.
- **Maker:** Ivan Murzak, trading as Modalith, a sole proprietorship in Kirkland, Washington (https://ai-game.dev/trust).
- **Age:** the Unity plugin has been open on GitHub since April 2025. The Godot and Unreal plugins followed in 2026.

### Pages read

- https://ai-game.dev/
- https://ai-game.dev/download
- https://ai-game.dev/pricing
- https://ai-game.dev/trust
- https://ai-game.dev/mcp-endpoint-info
- https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/installation
- https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/projects-and-engines
- https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/cli
- https://ai-game.dev/legal/terms (truncated, with a summary of the rest)
- https://ai-game.dev/legal/privacy (truncated, with a summary of the rest; the summary covers sections 2.13 and later, and the verbatim text does not reach section 2.13)

Not read: https://ai-game.dev/docs/tools, the Three.js page if one exists, https://ai-game.dev/docs/wiki/app/sign-in-and-account, https://ai-game.dev/model-availability, https://ai-game.dev/legal/refund, and https://discord.gg/cfbdMZX99G. Nothing was signed up for or downloaded.
